column9: My academic background and passion for scientific inquiry make me a strong candidate for this opportunity. I am eager to gain hands-on experience and contribute meaningfully to innovative projects.

Introduction & Motivation
Ever since I was a kid, I’ve been the kind of person who asks "Why?" a lot—why does the sky turn red at sunset? How do tiny cells come together to form life? What if we could solve energy crises with better technology? Science, to me, isn’t just a subject—it’s a way of questioning, experimenting, and discovering how the world works. That’s why I’m so excited about the Summer of Science (SoS) program. It’s the perfect opportunity to turn my classroom knowledge into real-world impact, work alongside passionate peers, and learn from mentors who share my curiosity.

Academic & Research Interests
I want to design experiments, collect data, and see theories come alive. I’m especially drawn to digital domain of VLSI because i find it very interesting and fun to learn. The SoS program, with its focus on hands-on research and mentorship, feels like the next big step in my journey.

Why I’m a Strong Fit for SoS
I like to solve puzzles: Whether it’s debugging code, optimizing a chemistry experiment, or figuring out why my physics model isn’t working, I don’t give up easily.

Teamwork is my favorite: Some of my best learning experiences have been in study groups or lab partners. I love bouncing ideas off others and believe great science happens through collaboration.

I’m Hungry to Learn: I may not know everything (who does?), but I’m always reading papers, watching lectures, or tinkering with side projects. SoS would be a chance to soak up knowledge from experts and peers alike.

What I Hope to Gain
Beyond just technical skills, I want to:

Fail and Learn: Research isn’t about being right—it’s about asking the right questions. I hope to embrace setbacks as part of the process.

Find My Niche: Maybe I’ll discover a passion for something I never knew I had!

Build Relationships: The chance to connect with professors and fellow science enthusiasts is priceless—I’d love to find mentors and maybe even future collaborators.

Closing
Science, to me, is more than formulas and data—it’s about wonder, persistence, and making a difference. If given the chance, I’ll bring my curiosity, hard work, and collaborative spirit to the SoS community. Thanks for considering my application—I’d be thrilled to be part of this adventure!

I’m excited to apply for the Summer of Science Project to explore and contribute to research in areas I’m genuinely passionate about—Aerodynamics, Fluid Mechanics, Combustion Engines, Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), Finite Element Analysis (FEA), and Robotics. As a Mechanical Engineering undergraduate at IIT Bombay, I’ve built a solid foundation in core subjects, especially through my course in Fluid Mechanics, which I found extremely fascinating. It helped me appreciate the physics behind flow, pressure, and energy, and made me realize how deeply fluids are connected to real-world problems—from flight to engines.

This curiosity led me naturally toward aerodynamics and CFD, where theory meets computation. Over time, I’ve gotten pretty comfortable using software like AutoCAD, Fusion 360, SolidWorks, ANSYS, and ADAMS. I’ve spent a lot of time modeling systems, running simulations, and trying to understand how fluid flow and mechanical motion can be predicted and improved through these tools.

One of my most involved projects was part of our ME 444 course. Our team built and analyzed a 5-degree-of-freedom pick-and-place robotic arm using ADAMS and Fusion. We did full kinematic and dynamic analysis, figuring out forces, torques, and joint behavior under different conditions. Honestly, it was intense, but also super rewarding. We also looked into a bunch of research papers to support our assumptions and tweak the design. That whole experience really boosted my understanding of robotics, system modeling, and gave me a taste of how theoretical concepts are tested in simulation and practice.

Outside academics, I’ve always been into cars and bikes, and that’s what got me interested in combustion engines. I’ve always wanted to dive deeper into how engines actually work—the fuel-air mix, combustion cycles, heat transfer, and how it all affects performance and efficiency. So, projects related to engine simulations or fluid-thermal systems are especially exciting to me, since they tie together my personal interests and academic direction.

This project feels like the perfect chance to explore these areas further in a research setting. I’m hoping to learn more about advanced simulation techniques, collaborate on interesting problems, and maybe get a taste of what actual research work feels like. I’m particularly drawn to projects where fluid mechanics is combined with mechanical design or robotics, because that’s where I feel I can contribute and learn the most.

Cybersecurity with AI (Artificial Intelligence) involves using machine learning, deep learning, and other AI techniques to enhance the protection of digital systems, networks, and data. Here's a breakdown of how AI is transforming cybersecurity:

### Key Applications of AI in Cybersecurity:

1. **Threat Detection and Prevention**  
   - AI can identify patterns in network traffic and user behavior to detect anomalies or potential threats (e.g., malware, phishing).
   - Machine learning models can analyze large volumes of data faster and more accurately than humans.

2. **Automated Response**  
   - AI can respond to incidents in real-time, such as isolating infected systems or blocking suspicious IP addresses.

3. **Security Analytics**  
   - AI helps security analysts by filtering out false positives and highlighting critical threats.

4. **Behavioral Analytics**  
   - AI models can build behavioral profiles for users and devices, flagging deviations that may indicate compromised accounts or insider threats.

5. **Fraud Detection**  
   - Common in banking and e-commerce, AI systems detect unusual transactions or login attempts.

6. **Threat Intelligence**  
   - AI can scan open web, dark web, and internal systems for new threats or leaked data.

### Benefits:
- Faster threat detection and response
- Reduced workload for human analysts
- Better accuracy over time with learning models

### Challenges:
- Adversarial AI: Hackers may use AI too, or design attacks that fool AI systems.
- Data privacy: AI requires access to large datasets, which may contain sensitive information.
- Model drift: AI models may become less effective over time without retraining.

I am Anant, a first-year undergraduate student in the IEOR (Industrial Engineering and Operations Research) program at IIT Bombay, with a CGPA of 9.3. I am excited to apply for the Summer of Science Project, driven by a strong interest in the intersection of human behavior, data analysis, and decision-making — particularly in the domains of social psychology and stock market analysis.

My interest in psychology was sparked through the HS112 Psychology course, which introduced me to the foundational principles of human behavior, cognitive biases, and social influence. The course allowed me to see how deeply psychological mechanisms affect our everyday decisions and how they can be modeled and studied systematically — especially in collective environments like markets and social groups.

What motivates me most is the opportunity to investigate how individuals and groups behave under uncertainty, and how these patterns influence larger systems. My academic background in IEOR, which emphasizes systems thinking, optimization, and statistical modeling, complements this interest well. I’m especially curious about how behavioral heuristics and social patterns influence financial markets and how data-driven approaches can uncover these dynamics.

My technical experience includes developing a Q-learning-based personalized news recommendation system, where I explored the exploration–exploitation trade-off in reinforcement learning, modeling user click behavior probabilistically. This project helped me understand how personalized decisions evolve and how behavioral tendencies can be learned and adapted to.

Currently, I am also working as a software trainee in Rakshak, contributing to a computer vision-based project, which has strengthened my technical grounding and collaborative skills. In addition, I’ve built a stochastic simulation model for emergency evacuation at railway stations, where I applied statistical tools to real-world human behavior scenarios under stress and crowding.

The Summer of Science Project offers an ideal platform for me to bring together my interest in psychology, data analysis, and complex systems. I look forward to learning from peers and mentors while contributing meaningfully to the research. I will supplement the learning with numerical simulations to make the theory concrete. I am deeply experienced in simulations, having created a realtime GPU physics solver: https://github.com/jjbel/samarium

I chose Device Physics as my first preference because Moore's Law is dying, and devices will soon stop getting faster. This is a crisis which can only be solved by research, which I hope to conduct someday.

Next I chose General Relativity and Fluid Mechanics, as simulating binary neutron star mergers is the most complex computer problem undertaken by man. It involves simulating all physical phenemona, from general relativity to quantum field theory. Telescope observations of jets are blind to the inner workings, which can only be explained by simulations. These will reveal deep truths about the formation and death of the universe.

Finally I chose neuroscience as I wish to understand how the inner workings of the brain can inspire Neural Network architectures, as well as neuromorphic computing.

My academic and intellectual curiosity lies at the intersection of neuroscience, machine learning, and systems engineering. I am particularly drawn to the challenge of decoding and modeling brain-like behavior in artificial systems, with an eye toward building technology that bridges biological intelligence and engineered computation. I also have a strong foundation in biology, having studied the subject in both class 11th and 12th, which has given me valuable insights into the workings of living systems.

Through SoS 2025, I hope to undertake a project that explores the core of real-time brain signal interpretation, aiming to develop adaptive systems that learn from and respond to neural patterns. Such a project not only requires a deep understanding of the brain itself but also demands rigorous modeling, efficient encoding of information, and robust hardware–software integration.

To support this vision, I have chosen the following topics:

Neuroscience (B14) to build a foundational understanding of brain structure and function.
Information Theory (E17) to study how neural signals can be effectively encoded, transmitted, and decoded.
Nonlinear Dynamical Systems (M33) to model complex, emergent behavior in neuronal activity.
Neural Networks (CS33) to design and train models that mimic learning and perception.
Machine Learning in Biology (B09) to explore how machine learning can be applied to biological data, including neural signals.

I intend to treat this project as a microcosm of a broader goal: creating systems that are inspired by the brain not just in form, but in function—systems that can learn, adapt, and interface seamlessly with human intent. I also plan to document progress through weekly summaries to build a well-structured, publishable final report.

The Summer of Science program offers the ideal platform to explore this multidisciplinary domain in both depth and direction.
